item.title: Bajcsy Awarded Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering
item.dc:creator: Mallory Lindahl
item.description:
Andrea Bajcsy, an assistant professor in Carnegie Mellon University's Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science, has received a 2026 Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering. The fellowship, awarded by the David and Lucile Packard Foundation, provides early career researchers with $985,834 in unrestricted funding over five years to pursue innovative research.

The post Peg-in-Hole Isn’t Kid Stuff appeared first on Robotics Institute Carnegie Mellon University.
item.content:encoded:
A rendering shows Northrop Grumman’s Mission Robotic Vehicle. (Northrop Grumman)

Placing a peg in a hole is literally child’s play, but when the peg and the hole are more than 22,000 miles above Earth the stakes are much higher. 

For Northrop Grumman, perfecting that peg-in-the-hole capability is key to a first-of-its-kind spacecraft designed to refuel and otherwise service satellites in geosynchronous orbit. A Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute (RI) team led by professor Howie Choset is providing its expertise to help the company achieve that goal.

Thousands of satellites now orbiting Earth aren’t functional, Choset said, most often because they simply ran out of fuel.

“There’s been this paradigm in aerospace, ‘launch once, use once,’” said Choset, the Kavčić-Moura Professor of Computer Science in the RI. “Now we’re poised to break that paradigm, so a satellite could remain in service indefinitely.”

Northrop Grumman operates several servicing spacecraft. Its most recent and advanced version, the Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), launched this past July from Cape Canaveral, Florida. 

Andrew Kwas, senior fellow at Northrop Grumman Space, said Choset and his students have been working with the company’s experts to devise a new technique that allows the MRV, which is about the size of a short school bus, to safely approach and dock with another satellite.

“Previously, satellites did not have an easy way to grapple and make a tight connection to allow refueling through a separate port to hold them stable for robotic operations,” Kwas said. “The new technique uses a probe that inserts into the nozzle of the target satellite’s liquid apogee engine to dock the spacecraft together.”

The liquid apogee engine is typically a spacecraft’s main engine.

The analytical and modeling support the Robotics Institute has provided for the new docking procedure has paid off in a big way, Kwas said.

“CMU and Northrop Grumman worked together to assess all contingencies for several years before the first successful mission,” Kwas said about using the new docking system. “Now the process has been repeatedly performed on orbit several times.”

To date, refueling has been the primary use for the servicing spacecraft. 

“With the introduction of the MRV, we also have the option to perform repairs, replace parts or perform upgrades in orbit,” Kwas said. “There are many missions that this capability enables. One is the ability to dislodge or repair a solar panel, another failure point on satellites.”

In working with Northrop Grumman engineers on modeling and testing this new approach, Choset drew upon his experience with previous peg-in-the-hole projects in the RI. Aligning a peg with a hole requires not only visual but also touch, or haptic, feedback. It’s a classic challenge in robotics.

Choset is widely known for his work on snake-like robots, such as those his team recently used in Venezuela to look for survivors in the rubble of the June earthquake there. 

Years ago, his then-student David Rollinson sought to build ever more sophisticated snakebots and devised a “series elastic actuator,” a motor that can measure the amount of force it applies. Rollinson is now the chief technology officer of HEBI Robotics, a company Choset founded in 2014.

“It’s just like your muscles: When you press on a table, your muscles deliver force, but they also feel the reaction force created by pressing on the table,” Choset said.      

In addition to inventing these special actuators, Choset’s group built a robotic testbed, called a holodeck, that uses two robotic arms on a rail to simulate how robots act in the weightlessness of space. 

All of this expertise and hardware makes CMU’s Robotics Institute uniquely equipped to tackle the peg-in-hole problem in space.      

“They showed us early on that they had the skills to perform the dynamic space operations necessary to refine our design,” Kwas said.

Choset suggested that solving the peg-in-hole problem could have major implications for space operations.

“You solve that and you can assemble structures in space. You can maintain structures in space,” he said.

This capability could unlock the potential to build spacecraft in orbit rather than on Earth, eliminating the need to survive the stresses of launching from Earth, Choset said.

Working with Northrop Grumman for several years has presented Choset with new opportunities, including two Space University Research Initiative grants from the U.S. Space Command. One of the grants supports the work with the company.

item.title: CMU Researchers Give Robots a Delicate Touch
item.dc:creator: Mallory Lindahl
item.description:

The post CMU Researchers Give Robots a Delicate Touch appeared first on Robotics Institute Carnegie Mellon University.
item.content:encoded:
The Breakdown

  • CMU researchers created a robotic fingertip to help robots handle delicate tasks without breaking fragile or tiny objects, such as pills and potato chips.  
  • The new fingertips attach directly to researchers’ DeltaHands device, adding multisensory versatility to a flexible, low-cost robotic hand.  
  • Each fingertip measures squeezing pressure and uses a plastic fingernail to capture microvibrations.

* * *

Carnegie Mellon Robotics Institute faculty Zeynep Temel (left) and Oliver Kroemer (right) observe a robotic hand equipped with new human-inspired sensing fingertips.

Researchers in the Carnegie Mellon University Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science designed a new type of robotic fingertip that combines multiple senses to handle small, delicate objects. The technology could help a robotic home assistant pick up a specific number of pills — a challenging task because the tiny objects are difficult to grasp and easy to break.

The low-cost, versatile fingertips are inspired by their human counterparts and include familiar elements like a fingernail. 

“Dexterity is a frontier area of robotics, and we’re making rapid progress,” said Oliver Kroemer, an associate professor in the Robotics Institute (RI). “However, fine manipulation is still very much an open challenge, and that’s why we wanted to focus on it.” 

The work builds on the team’s DeltaHands project, which received funding from the National Science Foundation to create a low-cost, highly customizable flexible robotic hand that could turn the pages of a book, grab an oddly shaped item or complete other tasks typically difficult for a robot. The robot can have anywhere from one to six finger-like devices and, because many components are 3D printed, can be easily modified for specific tasks. 

This research builds on the DeltaHands device, creating human-inspired fingertips that attach to it and add more versatility for manipulating objects. 

Researchers used a strain gauge and microphone to enable the robot to sense what it was grasping and make decisions about how to handle it. The strain gauge measures the squeezing pressure the finger applies so the hand knows exactly how hard it’s pinching. The contact microphone sits behind a tiny plastic fingernail, capturing high-frequency vibrations as the finger slides over an object or bumps into a surface. Wrapped in a soft silicone skin for grip, the setup lets the robot hear subtle textures, detect slipping and note hidden edges it may catch on. All told, it cost less than $100 per fingertip, compared to $800 to create a similar device from off-the-shelf products.

“We show how multimodal touch can directly support both perception and control during manipulation,” said Zhuowei Xu, an alumnus from the College of Engineering who worked on the project while completing his master’s degree in mechanical engineering “By combining force and vibrotactile sensing, the robot can interact with objects in different ways depending on the task: from adjusting its grasp when an object starts to slip, to locating fine features that are difficult to see, to actively identifying properties of objects that are completely hidden from vision and using that information to guide the next action.”

To test manipulation, researchers experimented with counting and unstacking paper cups; detecting the material composition of various items, like coarse fabric or wax paper, through micro-vibrations; and grasping fragile items, such as tofu cubes and potato chips. Counting and unstacking cups allowed researchers to test how the fingertips improved manipulation with blocked visuals. The nail on the fingertip, which protects the microphone, was able to slide along the edge of the cups and count them. The microphone allowed researchers to detect differences in materials’ microvibrations, learn from those differences and detect what kind of material it was touching. 

The fingertips enable a level of sensing and perception that opens the door for new ways a robotic assistant could help someone in their home.

“I don’t want a robot that does the fun things I enjoy doing around the house,” said Zeynep Temel, an associate professor in the Robotics Institute. “What I want is to be in my machine shop working on my own projects or in my kitchen working on a new recipe. And while I don’t want a robot doing that work for me, I’d love a helper robot that can hand me the right materials, one that knows the difference between a box of nails and a box of rubber bands or if the rice jar is empty or not.”

The researchers presented their work at the 2026 Intelligent Robots and Systems Conference last week in Pittsburgh. The team plans to continue developing this robotic hand, exploring how to expand sensing from the fingertips to the whole device. In addition to the members mentioned, the team included RI Ph.D. alumni Zilin Si and Kevin Zhang.
